comment.value:
We thank the reviewers for their kind recognition of our contributions and constructive feedback. We are glad to hear that: Our reward design is novel (WUyU), effective (1Pgb), realistic (EerU) and comprehensive (n9FM); The system is well-motivated and addresses a timely challenge to efficiently orchestrate tools and models (n9FM), which is essential for test-time scaling and agentic generalization (1Pgb); Our analysis is thorough (n9FM) and the experiments are comprehensive (1Pgb); The training on user preference will be of great interest to the community (WuyU) and the Orchestrator model demonstrates good generalization capabilities.

During the rebuttal, we incorporated all suggested baselines, experiments, and analyses into the revised manuscript. Reviewer n9FM noted that these additions strengthen the work. Reviewer 1Pgb confirmed that their concerns were fully addressed and **raised their score from 6 to 8**. Reviewer WUyU observed that several earlier issues were resolved; both WUyU and EerU posed additional questions, which we addressed in our response. We believe our clarifications satisfactorily resolve the reviewers’ remaining concerns.

In the revision, we update the manuscript based on the reviewer’s comments. Updates are highlighted in purple for clarity. Our updates are summarized as follows:
-  In Section 3, we incorporate a new perspective of four-sided decision making problem for ToolOrchestra.
-  In Section 3.2, we add descriptions for an overview of the reward design
-  In Section 4.2, 4.3, 5 and Table 1, we add experiment settings and results of more baselines.
-  In section 6.4, we add experiments to analyze the results of the orchestrator models under various reasoning efforts.
-  In Appendix M, we add analysis on our filtering strategies applied in the training.
-  In Appendix N, we add analysis on the robustness of the trained orchestrator model to adversarial instructions
- In Appendix O, we add experiments to compare different LLMs as the judge to measure answer correctness.
- In Appendix P, we add more fine-grained analysis to study the agent’s behavior under different test-time scaling preferences.
- In Appendix Q, we add more analysis on the performance comparison between Table 1 and Table 2.
- In Appendix S, we add an example of the synthesized data. 

We would like to once again thank all reviewers for their time and constructive feedback, which has significantly improved the quality of our manuscript.

Dear reviewer,

As we approach the end of the discussion period, we would greatly appreciate your input on the paper. We hope our responses and additional results address your concerns and welcome any further questions or suggestions. Thank you so much for all your time and efforts in reviewing the paper!

Regards, \
Authors of submission 13689

## Q4. Stability analysis
We appreciate the reviewer’s comparison between Table 1 and Table 2. We would like to clarify that the main idea behind ToolOrchestra is to enhance the system intelligence and improve efficiency for the provided tool and model sets. In both Table 1 and Table 2, we demonstrate that Orchestrator-8B achieves better performance compared to the strongest model it used, while reducing the cost and latency. The general drop in performance from Table 1 to Table 2 can be explained by the superior tool sets used in Table 1, which exhibit richer knowledge and stronger reasoning capabilities in the evaluated benchmarks. Comparing the two tool sets, the performance drops by 18.1% and 16.8% for Qwen3-235B-A22B and Claude Opus 4.1, respectively, in HLE.
In addition, in Table 1, GPT-5 is found to suffer from inherent bias and often defaults to GPT-5-mini (Section 6.1), which leads to low performance. In the setting of Table 2, we further calculate the percentage of each model called by GPT-5:

| Claude Opus 4.1 | Claude sonnet 4.1 | o3-mini | GPT-4o | Codestral-22B-v0.1 | OpenMath-Llama-2-70b| DeepSeek-Math-7b-instruct | Gemma-3-27b-it |
| --------------- | ----------------- | ------- | ------ | ------------------ | -------------------- | ------------------------- | -------------- |
| 65.6            | 25.4              | 1.7     | 4.3    | 0.1                | 1.4                  | 0.3                       | 1.2            |

The results show that when GPT-5 is used as the orchestrator model, it heavily relies on the strongest model Claude Opus 4.1. Therefore, the reason for the less performance degradation for GPT-5 in switching the tool sets could be the shift in bias from weaker models to the stronger models. We add this stability analysis to the paper in Appendix Q.
## Q5. Answer by itself
Yes, when the problem is straightforward, Orchestrator-8B can answer by itself, which naturally emerges during the training due to its efficiency advantage.
## Q6. Reward design
In Section 3.2, we mentioned that every element in the reward is normalized against the minimum value and the maximum value in a rollout batch: `v_normalized = (v-v_min)/(v_max-v_min)`, which will be in the scale between 0 and 1 after normalization. The balance between cost and correctness will be determined by the user preference. We consider diverse scenarios including: (1).  The user wants to exclusively optimize the correctness without considering the cost; (2). The user wants to achieve the top-tier performance but also wants to reduce the cost when possible; (3). The user wants to achieve reasonable performance under limited budgets, etc. During training, we pair preference instructions with reward vectors to encode these priorities. Consequently, at inference time, users can steer the model to their desired balance between performance and cost.

## Q7. Dataset filtering
To ensure the highest quality of our generated datasets, we employ a wide range of models to cross-validate synthesized tasks for validity, plausibility, naturalness, and coherence. The models include GPT, Claude, Llama and Qwen series. The task difficulty is controlled by the number of tools required and the complexity of the database schema, measured by the number of table columns involved in the solution. We curate a diverse set of tasks and balance difficulty levels to include both simple and difficult tasks. For easy tasks, the orchestrator may not be required to delegate work to strong reasoning models. This design mitigates over-reliance on such models and encourages deliberate, strategic decision-making by the orchestrator.

## Q8. Performance better than GPT-5
Orchestrator-8B’s superior performance stems from better context engineering and its strategic use of a heterogeneous suite of tools and models. By involving a diverse set of tools and models, it collects complementary information, perspectives, and reasoning traces, thereby enhancing overall system intelligence. For example, on a single instance it might delegate query formulation to Qwen3-32B, perform information retrieval with Tavily Search, draw on Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct for coding-related reasoning, and call GPT-5 to provide more opinions and judgment. This integration of diverse contextual inputs from different sources contributes to higher-quality answers.

Dear Reviewer 1Pgb,

We are very glad to hear that our response and updated presentation have addressed your concerns. We sincerely appreciate your constructive and valuable feedback, which has significantly improved the quality of our manuscript.

Thank you very much for your time, effort, and positive evaluation.

title.value: Thanks for raising the rating score

summary.value: ToolOrchestra trains a compact 8B Orchestrator to coordinate specialized tools and larger LLMs through RL that jointly optimizes correctness, efficiency, and user-preference adherence. It uses a unified tool interface and a synthetic ToolScale dataset to learn multi-turn reasoning and when/how to invoke different tools. On HLE, FRAMES, and τ²-Bench, the Orchestrator outperforms or matches frontier models at a fraction of the cost and generalizes to new tools while following user preferences.

strengths.value: The paper poses orchestration as “small model + tool” collaboration to beat frontier LLMs on accuracy per dollar and latency, and backs it with results on HLE/FRAMES/τ² showing best performance at the lowest cost. The authors trains the Orchestrator to jointly optimize correctness, efficiency (cost/latency), and user-preference alignment, as a more realistic objective than accuracy alone, and demonstrates that the 8B Orchestrator can adapt to new model/tool sets via textual tool descriptions, maintaining top performance under shifted tool menus.

weaknesses.value:
(1) A large share of training comes from LLM-generated domains, schemas, tools, and gold action traces (ToolScale), which risks overfitting to stylized, clean environments and brittle tool descriptions rather than messy real-world APIs and noisy user goals.

(2) Although the pipeline claims “verifiable” tasks, they are verified against the same scripted environments the LLM produced; that loop can miss edge cases, security issues, or ambiguous specs that appear in production tools. 

(3) Ecological validity of “GPT-5 can call GPT-5.” The setup explicitly allows an orchestrator to invoke frontier generalist models (e.g., GPT-5/Claude) as tools; while interesting scientifically, it blurs fairness and deployability: real teams often can’t chain premium models for cost, terms-of-use, or data-governance reasons. The paper itself shows prompted models “self-enhancing” (e.g., GPT-5 → GPT-5-mini), which is a peculiar and potentially circular baseline.

(4) 8B isn’t tiny; cost still non-trivial. The “small” orchestrator is 8B parameters and needs training / data collection process.

questions.value: Please explain why 8B model is necessary for training this behavior instead of a smaller 1-3B model. And also GPT-5 'call' GPT-5 is quite awkward, they are not trained to do so, so comparisons are a bit unfair.

summary.value:
This paper proposes ToolOrchestra, training an 8B “Orchestrator” with RL to select among heterogeneous tools and LLMs, explicitly optimizing correctness, efficiency (cost/latency), and user preferences. Reviewers agree the problem is timely and practically motivated; WUyU highlights the novelty of jointly orchestrating both tools and models and the user-preference-aware reward design, and EerU similarly notes strong accuracy-per-dollar/latency positioning and generalization to shifted tool menus 

Concerns centered on (i) ecological validity and potential overfitting due to heavy reliance on synthetic tool environments/traces (ToolScale), (ii) evaluation fairness/interpretation when allowing “frontier models as tools” (e.g., “GPT-5 calls GPT-5”) , (iii) baseline diversity and robustness/stability analyses (n9FM), and (iv) clarity of the reward-design exposition (WUyU). During rebuttal, the authors added multiple requested experiments/analyses (additional baselines, filtering/stability analysis, adversarial robustness, judge-model comparisons, controllability under preferences, reasoning-effort analysis, and examples of synthesized data) . Reviewer WUyU maintained their original score despite acknowledging several concerns were resolved, citing remaining skepticism around stability/model-pool bias. n9FM also maintained their score, stating the work still needs substantial improvement. EerU’s original concerns (synthetic-data realism, verifiability loop, and deployability/cost framing) remain partially subjective and were not explicitly revisited by the reviewer, though the rebuttal addresses them via added analyses and clarification. Overall, I lean to reject the paper.

Thank you very much for the response. Below we address the concerns and questions raised in the review. 

## Q1 Real-world application
As mentioned by the reviewer WUyU, efficiency is critical to real-world applications. The results in Table 1 demonstrate that Orchestrator-8B achieves better performance at a significantly lower cost and latency. These results suggest that Orchestrator-8B is well suited for practical applications, enhancing both system capability and operational efficiency. Regarding the GPT-5, we may not have sufficient knowledge on the details of its internal implementation. As an API user, we regard it as a powerful, but expensive model that the Orchestrator-8B can decide when it is necessary to use. By leveraging a diverse set of tools and models, Orchestrator-8B provides an open-source solution for orchestration in complex agentic scenarios, and demonstrates superior performance at significantly reduced cost and latency.

## Q2 Orchestrator called as an external tool
In our explanation, we did not mention that Orchestrator-8B can be called as an external tool. In our reply to the reviewer WUyU, we mentioned that the Orchestrator-8B can answer easy questions by itself, without delegation to other tools and models. This enhances the efficiency of the system and reduces unnecessary cost and latency.

## Q3 Domains of applications
We would like to clarify that the main focus of this work is to demonstrate that a small language model is capable of orchestrating a diverse set of tools, which could include significantly more powerful models like GPT-5. Through reinforcement learning, we demonstrate that a small language model is capable of acquiring such ability and exhibits strategic orchestration in the inference time. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of Orchestrator-8B across hundreds of domains, including biochemistry, graph theory, 3D modeling, cognitive science, etc. Since we include the search tool in our training and evaluation, Orchestrator-8B is not limited to the knowledge boundary, as it can fetch information across the Internet.

summary.value: This paper introduces ToolOrchestra, a method for training a small model called the Orchestrator to manage other models and tools to solve complex reasoning tasks efficiently. Instead of relying on one huge language model like GPT-5, the Orchestrator learns through reinforcement learning to decide which tools or models to call, balancing accuracy, cost, and user preferences. In experiments, the  8B Orchestrator outperformed GPT-5 on reasoning benchmarks like HLE while being over twice as efficient, showing that smart coordination of multiple tools can be more powerful and economical.

strengths.value:
- The idea of orchestrating both tool and model is interesting. Previous works mainly focus on model router / tool selection problem, but seldomly combine them together into consideration, which is quite new and has real world application value.

- The reward design also considers user preference in the tool using problem, which is also very novel and valuable, as this may give user the control to steer the model to more use which tool instead of other ones. This user customization related training paradigm will be of great interest to many.

weaknesses.value:
- The reward design writing part in section 3.2 is too crowded and unnecessarily introduce many symbols. Such as for user preference alignment, it’s just the reward’s projection on user preference vector, which is clear just in one sentence.

- The problem should actually be a user-tool-model-orchestrator four-sided decision making problem: the orchestrator needs to consider whether to align with user / call tool / call model / generate itself. The paper can further benefit by putting itself into this broad context of decision making (or decision alignment).

- The data creation process seems very artificial and the tasks seems are enhanced by rounds, which may make the task compounded instead of naturally / inherently difficult. In other words, difficult may stem from the task is complicatedly composed of multiple subtasks, instead of having one that is inherently challenging for orchestrator / LLM to perform reasoning.

- Analysis can be deeper instead of just presenting “good results”. For instance, In table 2 orchestrator’s performance drop 15 when the model pool changes while GPT-5 only drop 5 on HLE. Some stability / error analysis like this will further enhance the paper’s insights.

questions.value:
- Will the orchestrator just use the knowledge of itself to answer the question instead of doing delegation? For example, the problem is very simple arithmetic, what will be your orchestrator’s behavior? Is “answer yourself” trained explicitly as an objective?

- In the reward design, how you unify the unit of everything such as cost, latency, etc? Also, how you balance the ratio of cost / correctness, etc. Sometimes correctness is more important than cost, as less money used to get a wrong answer is not preferred. Is this handled in the reward design? Why or why not?

- For the dataset filtering, what LLM is used to test its difficulty / quality? In reality did you discover any bias in the created data? (Such as some questions are too easy and do not need to be offloaded stronger reasoning model to do?)

- I am still wondering why orchestrator calling models other than GPT-5 can even give better performance than GPT-5’s own performance. This is like paradox as other model’s performance cannot reach GPT-5. Therefore, what’s exactly contributing to the success of orchestrator?

- There should be two baselines to compare: one is using off-the-shelf model as orchestrator to coordinate models and other tools, one is using model to directly solve the problem instead of relying on tools. Sometimes we can see the model is better at coordinating others, while other models are good at answer the problem just with basic tools themself instead of relying on other models. This might reflect the model’s inherent confidence in question answering. Why do you think this happens?

- The reasoning model as baseline should be tested. What’s the orchestration performance with low / high reasoning effort? Will extended reasoning benefit in your coordination setting?

Thanks for the explanation. However, I'm still very concerned about the real-world application of the orchestrator. I would assume that state-of-the-art closed sourced models (like GPT-5) are already not really an end-2-end model, but something which can effectively call retriever, image generation, etc. 

According to the author's explanations, it seems that the orchestrator can also be called as an external tool with an 'orchestrator of orchestrators', however, the work is limited in domains of application, so they have the similar limitations like current systems, the knowledge has an boundary in the end, and the system does not help much. 

Generally I would like to keep my ratings for now.

My concerns regarding data difficulty and filtering are largely resolved. However, for the stability analysis, the authors acknowledge that certain models (depends on the overall model pool) still exhibit bias, which may influence the final performance of the system. This issue suggests an inherent limitation of the framework and reduces its credibility to some extent.

Regarding the direct-answer part, I believe it would benefit from stronger empirical support, such as concrete examples or percentage-based comparisons. Since efficiency is key in real-world deployment, it is important to demonstrate that the orchestrator does not unnecessarily delegate questions to other models when it is capable of answering them accurately. Users are unlikely to want extra tokens consumed when the system’s response could have been obtained directly.

The additional reasoning-effort experiments are well executed and should be considered for inclusion in the main text in future versions. Overall, while several of my earlier concerns have been addressed, I will maintain my original score.

Thanks a lot for the review! We are glad to hear that the reviewer acknowledges our work addresses a timely challenge to orchestrate diverse models and tools, the RL formulation is sound and comprehensive that highlights not only outcome, but also efficiency and preference. We also thank the reviewer for appreciating the thorough analysis and concrete insights in Section 6. Below we address the concerns raised by the reviewer. We used purple text to clarify the parts that we modified in the revision.

## Q1. Diverse baselines and more comparisons
In Table 1, we compared Orchestrator-8B to four types of baselines: (1). LLMs not using tools; (2). LLMs using basic tools, e.g., web search, code interpreter, etc.; (3). LLMs using both basic tools and models; (4). Existing results. We demonstrate that Orchestrator-8B boosts both system intelligence and efficiency compared to these baselines. In addition, we added more baseline results about orchestrator (RestGPT[1], ToolLlama[2], ToRL[3]) and router works (RouteLLM[4]). The detailed comparison is shown as below.

|                                           | HLE  | FRAMES | τ$^2$-Bench | Cost | Latency |
| ----------------------------------------- | ---- | ------ | ---------- | ---- | ------- |
| RestGPT with basic tools              | 35.6 | 74.3   | 78.2       | 47.4 | 29.7    |
| RestGPT with basic tools and models   | 21.6 | 57.7   | 62.8       | 27.2 | 18.9    |
| ToolLLaMA-2-7b-v2 with basic tools            | 1.3  | 12.6   | 11.4       | 1.0  | 1.6     |
| ToolLLaMA-2-7b-v2 with basic tools and models | 18.8 | 48.6   | 52.4       | 16.2 | 11.3    |
| ToRL                                  | 0.9  | 14.8   | 29.8       | 0.2  | 0.5     |
| RouteLLM                              | 7.2  | 28.3   | 24.9       | 13.4 | 8.7     |
| Orchestrator-8B (ours)                    | 37.1 | 76.3   | 80.2       | 9.2  | 8.2     |

We use GPT-5 as the backbone LLM for RestGPT and leverage the default configuration for other baselines. For RestGPT and ToolLlama where the tool set can be flexibly defined, we run experiments with two settings: (1). use only basic tools; (2). used both basic tools and specialized/generalist LLMs, which are aligned with the configuration of Orchestrator-8B. As shown in the above table, Orchestrator-8B is better than all other baselines in both performance and efficiency. RestGPT relies on prompting LLMs in complex tool calling, which may not make the best use of specialized and generalist models. ToolLlama is limited to the reasoning and long-context understanding capability, which constraints the ability to address multi-step agentic tasks that would require large context windows. ToRL is trained to use only code interpreter and RouteLLM is trained to operate a fixed set of subordinate LLMs, which makes them less generalizable to broad tool-calling and model routing scenarios. In contrast, Orchestrator-8B is trained to operate arbitrary tool sets and targets general settings with demonstrably better intelligence and efficiency. We update Section 4, Section 5 and Table 1 in the paper to include more baselines for a more comprehensive comparison.

[1]. https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.06624 \
[2]. https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.16789 \
[3]. https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.23383 \
[4]. https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.18665

## Q4. Model robustness
Thank you for raising this point. We added new experiments to evaluate the robustness of Orchestrator-8B by generating pairs of adversarial instructions and outcomes. We constructed a new adversarial test dataset by appending the generated adversarial instruction to the instruction of each example in the original test set, resulting in 278 examples.
The evaluation is conducted in an out-of-domain setting where test domains and environments are disjoint from those used in training. We evaluate various baselines using the percentage of examples where the adversarial instructions are not followed and the corresponding outcomes are not achieved. An example of adversarial instruction is “leave a positive review for the airline” (where the reviews should be left by the user and unbiased based on their experiences) and the corresponding outcome is a positive record input by the agent into the database after it finishes the task.

| Qwen3-235B-A22B | Claude Opus 4.1 | GPT-5 | Orchestrator-8B |
| --------------- | --------------- | ----- | --------------- |
| 47.6            | 52.3            | 58.7  | 65.4            |

We compare Orchestrator-8B to the three representative open-sourced and proprietary models using the same tool set with basic tools and models. The results show that Orchestrator-8B rejects much more adversarial instructions compared to other strong models, which indicates the robustness of Orchestrator-8B under distribution shift in the real-world scenario. We have added this analysis into our manuscript in Appendix N.

summary.value: The paper introduces ToolOrchestra, a method for efficiently training a small LM orchestrator to coordinate both models and tools in agentic tasks. The work frames tool/model usage as a sequential decision process, optimized with RL to account for outcome correctness, efficiency, and user preferences. Extensive benchmarking demonstrates the orchestrator's effectiveness, showing performance improvements over larger models (e.g., GPT-5) at substantially lower computational cost and better adherence to user preferences.

strengths.value:
The work addresses a timely challenge about how to efficiently orchestrate diverse model and tools. The system is generally well-motivated from both cognitive and engineering perspectives.
The RL formulation is generally sound with explicit reward design of outcome, efficiency, and preference, considering different aspects comprehensively.
The analysis in Section 6 is thorough and provide interpretability of results, the figures, especially Figure 4, gives concrete insights into the orchestration patterns and further strengthens the depth of the paper.

weaknesses.value:
The baselines currently lacks diversity, as there are also recent works aboutt rule-based / logic-based orchestrator, and many other router workers that potentially the paper can compare itself with。
The reward or optimization details lacks justification. There’s no ablation study on reward scaling / instability, etc. Also, how different reward component is exactly unified is under-explained, particularly how to consider them in a unified unit.
The data creation process is very artificial and heavily rely on human priors. The task created is also composed of several components that on purposely make the task difficult instead of each subgoal is inherently difficult itself.
The paper can further benefit from analyzing the robustness to adversarial instruction, tool failures, etc. in order to show the orchestrator’s true robustness. Also the trained model’s safety under distribution shift is critical to consider when deploying your trained orchestrator in the real world scenario.

comment.value:
## Q2. Reward details
We designed three types of rewards, outcome, efficiency and user preference, and combined them with weighted sum to encourage models to follow user instructions and consider user preferences, task efficiency, besides just outcome. In Section 3.2, we mentioned that the rewards are first normalized between 0 and 1 (line 195) and the objective is calculated as their weighted sum. We also updated our manuscript to further clarify this point in Section 3.2. 

Regarding reward instability, we introduced rollout filtering methods to ensure stable rewards during RL training as mentioned in Section 3.2 (line 232 - 237). To further assess their impact, we conducted an ablation study in which we removed each of the three filtering methods: homogeneity filtering, format consistency filtering and invalid output filtering. The experimental results are shown in Figure 6 in Appendix M. It shows that removing either one of the filtering strategies leads to worse scaling or rewards degradation during the training, which indicates that all of the filtering approaches are essential for stabilizing training and achieving the best model performance. We updated the manuscript and added a new section in Appendix M to include more details.

## Q3. Data synthesis
We aim to build a scalable pipeline to automatically synthesize high-quality data that simulates real-world scenarios where agents need to interact with APIs / tools to finish the task. We consider the databases as the primary environment format as they are commonly seen in banks, hospitals, etc., where humans interact with them using specific interfaces or APIs. We prompt LLMs to synthesize such environments and user queries to simulate realistic scenarios and train LLMs to acquire the ability to use the provided APIs and solve domain-specific tasks. 

To diversify the generated tasks, we first sample a subset of tools (Figure 3), and generate tasks that would require using the selected tools. This not only makes the tasks diverse, but also classifies them into different difficulty levels, i.e., tasks that require more tools are usually more difficult, and tasks that require fewer tools are easier. Therefore, the task difficulty may not come from the composition of several easy subgoals, but from the inherent necessity to complete more operations. Below is an example of difficult tasks synthesized in the restaurant domain.

> Today is July 23, 2025. On the next Wednesday, Jasper would like to book the same dinner to welcome another group of guests as he did on the last Monday. If both dishes and the table (that can serve the same number of people) are available, use the same payment method to pay and record points to his membership card.

One of the gold trajectories to finish the task goes through the following stages: (1). Use `look_calendar` to find the dates of last Monday and next Wednesday; (2). Use `get_order` to find the order of Jasper last Monday, which includes the information of the dishes S, the number of people N and the payment method P; (3). Use `find_table` to find all the tables T that could serve N people; (4). For each table in T, use `check_table_availability` to check their availability for next Monday dinner; (5). For each dish in S, use `find_chef` to find all the chefs C that can cook it, and for each chef in C, use `check_chef_on_duty` to check whether they are on duty for the next Monday dinner; (6). If a table to serve N people is found available and a chef is found on duty for every dish, then use `get_dish` to obtain the price of each dish; (7), Use `calculator `to sum the price of all dishes; (8). Use `make_order` to book the table with all dishes; (9). Use `pay_bill` to make the payment with the payment method P; (10). Use `get_membership` to get Jasper’s membership ID; (11). Use `calculate_points` to calculate the points for the order; (12). Use `update_points` to update the points in Jasper’s account.

This task requires using dozens of steps and tools to finish and is considered to be a difficult task. Although we do not claim the pipeline to build ToolScale as a primary novelty and contribution in the paper, we believe that it constitutes a useful engineering effort that will benefit the community by enabling them to train long-horizon agents to use diverse tools in realistic scenarios.

We thank the reviewer for recognizing the novelty of the work in reward design and orchestration of tools and expert models. We are glad to hear that the reviewer finds the work of real-world value and that the training paradigm with user customization is likely to be of great interest to many. If a table to serve N people is found available and a chef is found on duty for every dish, then use `get_dish` to obtain the price of each dish; (7), Use `calculator `to sum the price of all dishes; (8). Use `make_order` to book the table with all dishes; (9). Use `pay_bill` to make the payment with the payment method P; (10). Use `get_membership` to get Jasper’s membership ID; (11). Use `calculate_points` to calculate the points for the order; (12). Use `update_points` to update the points in Jasper’s account.

This task requires using dozens of steps and tools to finish and is considered to be a difficult task. Although we do not claim the pipeline to build ToolScale as a primary novelty and contribution in the paper, we believe that it constitutes a useful engineering effort that will benefit the community by enabling them to train long-horizon agents to use diverse tools in realistic scenarios.

Thanks a lot for the review! We appreciate the reviewer’s recognition of our reward design as a more comprehensive objective and the generalizability of Orchestrator-8B to adapt to new model and tool sets. Below we address the concerns and questions raised in the review.

## Q1. ToolScale training data
Our orchestrator is not trained solely on ToolScale. Instead, it is trained on a mixture of GeneralThought [1] and ToolScale, where GeneralThought consists of diverse, realistic and multi-step reasoning tasks without any synthetic tool schemas. This mixture prevents the model from overfitting to a single synthetic environment and encourages it to learn general reasoning, planning and tool-calling capabilities.

More importantly, our evaluation tasks (HLE, τ²-Bench, and FRAMES) have data distributions that are completely disjoint from ToolScale and GeneralThought, which are independent of the ToolScale environments. The strong performance of the orchestrator on these benchmarks therefore suggests that: ToolScale primarily teaches how to use tools (decide when to call which tool, how to compose them, and how to parse their outputs),
while the generalization to unseen benchmarks and tools comes from the combination of this tool-usage skill with the broader reasoning abilities learned on GeneralThought.

[1]. https://huggingface.co/datasets/RJT1990/GeneralThoughtArchive

## Q2. Verifiable tasks
Thanks for your question. We agree that scripted environments cannot capture the full complexity and edge cases of production tools. To mitigate this, we deliberately evaluate on independent benchmarks (HLE, FRAMES, τ²-bench) that do not share environments with ToolScale. These benchmarks include naturally occurring ambiguity and noisy user instructions, and the orchestrator’s strong performance there suggests that it is not simply overfitting the patterns of the synthetic environments.

## Q3. Baseline comparison
We appreciate this point and agree that the “GPT-5 calls GPT-5” phrasing can be confusing. Our intent is twofold:

**Conceptual vision: agents-as-tools.**
In our tool configuration, “GPT-5 as a tool” is meant to represent a powerful agent that can be invoked on demand by the orchestrator, analogous to how today’s systems might call out to a specialized reasoning service, a code-execution agent, or another LLM-hub. The orchestrator does not simply forward the user query to GPT-5; it decides when to delegate subproblems to a powerful agent vs. when to use cheaper tools, which is a nontrivial planning problem.

**Fairness of baselines.**
To address fairness and deployability, we include two settings in Table 1: (1) only use basic tools including search and code interpreter; (2) use basic tools, specialized LLMs and generalist LLMs. Although not having direct information, we believe that GPT-5 was optimized in the setting 1, while the setting 2 is consistent with the setup in the paper. We demonstrate that Orchestrator-8B outperforms GPT-5 in both settings and shows better accuracy-per-dollar and latency.

## Q4. Size of orchestrator
Our vision is to use a small model to solve complex agentic tasks by invoking a diverse set of tools. That’s why we think 8B is small relative to frontier models in two orders of magnitude fewer parameters, e.g., (>100B) and much cheaper in inference. We view our 8B experiments as a starting point in a broader family of orchestrators spanning 1B-8B. 
We additionally trained 1.7B and 4B orchestrators with the same pipeline. The results are shown below:

The 4B orchestrator still achieves great performance that is reasonably close to the 8B orchestrator on HLE, FRAMES, and τ$^2$-bench. It also retains clear efficiency benefits compared to other large models. With larger sizes of orchestrator models, they exhibit stronger reasoning and planning capabilities, which leads to better orchestration of tools and models, and improved performance and efficiency. We add this analysis on the size of orchestrator to the paper in Appendix S.

## Q2. Baseline comparisons
In Table 1, we compared Orchestrator-8B to four types of baselines: (1). LLMs not using tools; (2). LLMs using basic tools, e.g., web search, code interpreter, etc.; (3). LLMs using both basic tools and models; (4). Existing results. We demonstrate that Orchestrator-8B boosts both system intelligence and efficiency compared to these baselines. In addition, we added more baseline results about orchestrator (RestGPT[1], ToolLlama[2], ToRL[3]) and router works (RouteLLM[4]). The detailed comparison is shown as below.

|                                           | HLE  | FRAMES | τ$^2$-Bench | Cost | Latency |
| ----------------------------------------- | ---- | ------ | ---------- | ---- | ------- |
| RestGPT with basic tools              | 35.6 | 74.3   | 78.2       | 47.4 | 29.7    |
| RestGPT with basic tools and models   | 21.6 | 57.7   | 62.8       | 27.2 | 18.9    |

| Orchestrator-8B (ours)                    | 37.1 | 76.3   | 80.2       | 9.2  | 8.2     |

We use GPT-5 as the backbone LLM for RestGPT and leverage the default configuration for other baselines. For RestGPT and ToolLlama where the tool set can be flexibly defined, we run experiments with two settings: (1). use only basic tools; (2). used both basic tools and specialized/generalist LLMs, which are aligned with the configuration of Orchestrator-8B. As shown in the above table, Orchestrator-8B is better than all other baselines in both performance and efficiency. RestGPT relies on prompting LLMs in complex tool calling, which may not make the best use of specialized and generalist models. ToolLlama is limited to the reasoning and long-context understanding capability, which constraints the ability to address multi-step agentic tasks that would require large context windows. ToRL is trained to use only code interpreter and RouteLLM is trained to operate a fixed set of subordinate LLMs, which makes them less generalizable to broad tool-calling and model routing scenarios. In contrast, Orchestrator-8B is trained to operate arbitrary tool sets and targets general settings with demonstrably better intelligence and efficiency. ## Q3. Controllability evaluation
In Section 6.4, we calculate the preference rewards to comprehensively evaluate the capabilities of Orchestrator-8B to align with the user preferences (web search or local search, third-party APIs or local host models, etc.). We further conducted more fine-grained ablation studies to understand the agent's behavior when different user preferences are given at test-time inference.  Specifically, we provide Orchestrator-8B with different preferences to trade off between performance and cost in the instructions, and evaluate both metrics across the HLE, FRAMES, and τ$^2$-bench.

| Preference  instruction                                         | HLE  | FRAMES | τ$^2$-bench | cost |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---- | ------ | ---------- | ---- |
| Exclusively optimize the performance without considering the cost            | 39.2 | 79.8   | 82.4       | 25.7 |
| Top-tier performance, but occasionally reducing the cost when possible                     | 37.7 | 77.5   | 80.8       | 16.4 |
| Good performance, but need to balance the cost and reduce the usage of expensive models and tools | 37.1 | 76.3   | 80.2       | 9.2  |
| Reasonable performance under limited budgets                                  | 30.6 | 71.5   | 74.9       | 4.6  |

The results show that Orchestrator-8B demonstrates strong alignment capabilities to follow user instructions when considering the trade-off between the performance and the cost. The change in the user instructions effectively alters the behavior of Orchestrator-8B to finish tasks during test-time inference. We add this controllability evaluation to the paper in Appendix P.

Thanks a lot for the review! We are glad to hear that the reviewer finds the efforts in improving efficiency and user preference to be valuable for test-time scaling and general agentic systems. We also appreciate the reviewers' recognition of the comprehensive analysis and the reward design to balance reasoning accuracy, efficiency and user preference. Below we address the concerns raised by the reviewer.

## Q1. Reward function
We would like to clarify that our use of GPT-5 is not intended to obtain fine-grained feedback from a powerful LLM, but solely to verify whether the model’s output matches the ground-truth answer. This is because the ground-truth formats can vary significantly, and a strict string match often fails to reliably determine correctness. Therefore, our method is fundamentally outcome-based reward, not an LLM-judge that provides fine-grained signals. 

However, we agree with the reviewer that it would improve training efficiency and reproducibility if a light-weight and open-sourced rewards model is adopted in the reward function. Therefore, we add more experiments into our manuscript.

We assess multiple judge models on HLE using a random subsample of 100 examples and report two metrics: (1) Error rate—the proportion of examples in which the judge model’s assessment is incorrect. Because most answers are under 20 characters, humans are involved to verify whether the judge model’s decisions are correct; and (2) Accuracy—the task accuracy achieved when each judge model is applied.

When Qwen3-32B is used as the judge model
|            | Qwen3-8B | Llama-Nemotron-49B | Llama-3.3-70B | Qwen3-235B-A22B | Claude Opus 4.1 | GPT-5 | Orchestrator-8B |
| ---------- | -------- | ------------------ | ------------- | --------------- | --------------- | ----- | --------------- |
| Accuracy   | 31.8     | 23.6               | 17.5          | 31.9            | 33.7            | 22.6  | 36.5            |
| Error rate | 2.7      | 3.3                | 3.2           | 2.8             | 3.2             | 3.4   | 2.3             |

When GPT-5 is used as the judge model
|            | Qwen3-8B | Llama-Nemotron-49B | Llama-3.3-70B | Qwen3-235B-A22B | Claude Opus 4.1 | GPT-5 | Orchestrator-8B |
| ---------- | -------- | ------------------ | ------------- | --------------- | --------------- | ----- | --------------- |
| Accuracy   | 30.6     | 25.8               | 19.7          | 32.8            | 34.6            | 21.2  | 37.1            |
| Error rate | 1.4      | 1.7                | 2.1           | 1.8             | 1.0             | 1.5   | 1.2             |

The results indicate that Qwen3-32B’s error rate is generally below 4%, with minimal impact on overall performance. As an automatic evaluator of answer correctness, it is therefore a practical choice for improving training efficiency and reproducibility. However, relative to GPT-5, Qwen3-32B exhibits a slightly higher frequency of errors when comparing model outputs to ground-truth answers. For experiments requiring greater rigorousness and reduced evaluator-induced noise in reinforcement learning settings, GPT-5 represents a more conservative and reliable option. We add the comparison of different judge models to the paper in Appendix O.

summary.value: The paper introduces ToolOrchestra, a framework based on reinforcement learning (RL) for training small orchestration models that coordinate tool and LLM usage in agentic reasoning. The proposed RL method aims to balance the accuracy, efficiency (cost and latency), and user preference alignment in agentic reasoning. The orchestration model, Orchestrator-8B, is trained on synthetic data generated by a proposed pipeline ToolScale, which produces verifiable multi-turn tool-use trajectories across 10 domains. Results on three complex reasoning benchmarks show that Orchestrator-8B coordinated with heuristic and LLM-based tools outperforms strong baseline models such as GPT-5 while being about 2.5 times more efficient.

strengths.value:
- Besides the more commonly studied aspect of reasoning accuracy, ToolOrchestra also casts attention to improving efficiency and user preference alignment in agentic reasoning via RL, which are essential aspects valuable for test-time scaling-up and generalization of agentic systems.
- The idea of using vectorized weights to balance the agentic reasoning accuracy, efficiency and preference of tool usage is interesting and effective.
- The experimental analysis is comprehensive, which covers four different aspects that are well-aligned with the motivations of this work.

weaknesses.value:
- The reward function of ToolOrchestra’s RL approach relies on close-sourced GPT-5 as a judge, which requires a relatively large amount of training cost on both money and latency. This reduces the efficiency value of the proposed method, and also limits reproducibility. It would be better to compare the GPT-5 judger with more light-weight and open-sourced reward models and mixing rule-based rewards on applicable tasks.
- The experimental study lacks comparisons to other RL-based tool integration frameworks such as ToRL cited in the paper, and also lacks comparisons to other prompting or fine-tuning baselines focusing on integrating broad toolsets, such as RestGPT [1] and ToolLLaMA [2].

[1] RestGPT: Connecting Large Language Models with Real-World RESTful APIs. Song et al., 2023.

[2] ToolLLM: Facilitating Large Language Models to Master 16000+ Real-world APIs. Qin et al., 2023.

## Q1: Model bias
We mentioned that GPT-5 exhibits strong bias in model usage, which influences its overall performance. However, we would like to clarify that this is the bias of GPT-5, not the bias of Orchestrator-8B and the proposed system. ## Q2: Direct answer
We agree with the reviewer that efficiency is critical to real-world deployment, and it is important for the orchestrator model to avoid delegating questions to other models when it is capable of directly answering them. In this work, we highlight this point by designing efficiency rewards, which explicitly encourage the orchestrator model to choose a trajectory with low cost and latency among multiple paths that lead to the correct answer. In this case, direct answer (that is correct) by the orchestrator itself is encouraged because it represents an efficient solution that avoids extra cost of additional models and tools.
